A cleft is a narrow crack, split, or opening in something solid — the kind of gap that appears when a surface or object has been divided or split apart, but not completely separated into two separate pieces.

Imagine a large rock face on a cliff. Over thousands of years, pressure and erosion cause it to crack. The two halves haven't fallen apart — they're still essentially one rock — but there's now a narrow, deep gap running through it. That gap is a cleft.

The key feel of a cleft is this: something that was once whole now has a split running through it, and the result is a narrow, often deep, opening. Think of it as the result of something being cleaved (split) — which is exactly where the word comes from in spirit.
What makes a cleft distinct from similar words

This is where precision really matters:

  • A crack is similar, but it's more informal and usually refers to something accidental or structural. A cleft has a more deliberate, clean quality to it — it can be natural or biological, and it often implies the split has some depth and definition.
  • A crevice is almost identical to a cleft in most situations (both refer to a narrow gap in rock or earth), but "crevice" is almost always used for geology — rocks, glaciers, walls. A cleft is broader: it applies to rocks, body parts, trees, and more.
  • A fissure is also a crack or split, but the word leans scientific and medical. A fissure in rock, a fissure in the skin. A cleft has a slightly more visual, descriptive quality.
  • A groove is a channel cut into a surface — it's a deliberate indent running along something, usually made by a tool. A cleft is not a groove: a cleft goes into the material as a split, not along the surface.
  • A gap is simply an open space between two separate things. A cleft is specifically a split within one thing — the two sides of a cleft are still part of the same object.
Where you'll encounter the word — by context

1. In nature and geography

A cleft in a rock is a narrow split in the rock face, deep enough to cast a shadow, wide enough perhaps to slide a hand into or to shelter inside. Hikers and climbers often refer to clefts in cliffs or boulders. A river can flow through a cleft in a mountain range — that narrow passage carved between steep walls.

"He wedged his rope into the cleft in the granite to secure his climb."

2. In the human body (anatomy and medicine)

This is one of the most common uses:

  • A cleft palate is a split in the roof of the mouth (the palate) that some babies are born with — a gap that runs down the middle of the palate because the two sides didn't fuse together properly during development. It requires surgery to repair.
  • A cleft lip (sometimes called a "harelip," though that term is considered outdated) is a similar split — a narrow gap in the upper lip, also present from birth.
  • A cleft chin is that small vertical indentation or dimple you see in the middle of some people's chins — like a tiny groove or notch in the chin caused by the underlying muscle and bone structure. It's the same concept: a split in the surface, here a natural physical feature rather than a medical condition.

"The actor was known for his strong jaw and distinct cleft in his chin."

3. In trees and wood

A cleft in a tree refers to the split where a trunk divides into two branches, or a deep crack in the bark and wood. Gardeners and botanists use "cleft grafting" — a technique where a small split (a cleft) is made in a branch, and a new cutting is inserted into it to grow.

"The old oak had a deep cleft where lightning had struck it decades ago."
The qualities a cleft always has

Whenever you see "cleft" used as a noun, you can be sure of these things:

  • Narrowness: A cleft is not a wide-open space. It's tight, confined, and narrow relative to its depth. Something could be wedged into a cleft, or peer through a cleft — because it's narrow enough to give that sense of a tight passage or opening.
  • Depth: Unlike a scratch or a surface mark, a cleft goes inward. It has some depth to it — enough to make it a meaningful opening, not just a line on the surface.
  • One thing, not two: The two sides of a cleft are still part of the same object. This is what separates a cleft from a gap between two separate objects.
  • A result of splitting: A cleft is always the product of something being divided — by nature, by force, by growth, or by birth. It carries the idea of something having been split.
A quick set of example sentences to seal the idea

• "The explorers found fresh water trickling through a cleft in the limestone."
  • "She ran her finger along the cleft in the old wooden table, feeling the grain of the wood on either side."
  • "The surgeon specialised in repairing cleft palates in newborns."
  • "A narrow shaft of sunlight entered through the cleft between the canyon walls."
  • "His grandfather had a deep cleft in his chin — the same one he had inherited."

A cleft is a narrow, often deep split or crack in something solid — the gap left behind when something is divided but not completely separated, seen in rocks and cliffs, in the human body (like a cleft palate or a cleft chin), and in trees.
